files.lesson.md: --- order: 9 unit: fractions node: AC9M7N04 n1 assumes: [AC9M4N03 n1] title: Equivalent fractions summary: "Fractions are equal when they shade the same amount. Multiply or divide the top and the bottom by the same number: 2/3 = 4/6 = 8/12. Dividing by the highest common factor gives the simplest form." language: maths voice: { name: af_heart, speed: 1.1 } hook: "Half a pizza cut into 2 slices or into 8: the same amount to eat. The numbers change; the amount does not." app: command: node "$REPO_ROOT/tools/serve.mjs" "$REPO_ROOT/dist/_playground-board" 8173 url: http://127.0.0.1:8173/index.html readySelector: "#sl-c" layout: full explainPicture: { ref: bars.yml#explain-pic, caption: "$\\tfrac{2}{3} = \\tfrac{8}{12}$: each third is split into 4, so the top and the bottom are both multiplied by 4." } explainClip: query: { code: "@bars.yml#explain", fresh: 1, id: explain } caption: "The same amount, more parts" say: "Equal fractions shade the same amount." clip: - caption: { text: "2/3: 2 of 3 equal parts.", say: "Two thirds: two of three equal parts." } - wait: 500 - caption: { text: "Split every part in 2: 6 parts, 4 shaded. 2/3 = 4/6.", say: "Split every part in two. Six parts, four shaded: the same amount." } - click: Make d bigger - click: Make d bigger - click: Make d bigger - click: Make c bigger - click: Make c bigger - expect: { selector: "#gsum", contains: "2/3 = 4/6" } - wait: 600 - caption: { text: "× 2 on the top and the bottom.", say: "Times two on the top and the bottom." } - wait: 1200 --- A fraction names an amount: $\tfrac{5}{8}$ is 5 of 8 equal parts. The top number is the **numerator** (how many parts) and the bottom number the **denominator** (how many equal parts in the whole); here they're just the top and the bottom. The same amount can be cut into more parts, or fewer, and named by a different fraction. Fractions that name the same amount are **equivalent**. Fraction bars show which fractions are equivalent, and they also show the one with the fewest parts: the **simplest form**. ## Predict: the same as 2/3 ```step stage: predict insight: "Committing to a fraction equal to 2/3 shows whether they multiply both numbers or add the same number to both." check: type: predict q: "Which fraction is the same amount as $\\tfrac{2}{3}$?" options: - "$\\tfrac{4}{6}$" - "$\\tfrac{3}{4}$" - "$\\tfrac{2}{6}$" - "$\\tfrac{4}{5}$" actual: "4/6. Split each third into 2: 6 parts, and the 2 shaded thirds become 4 shaded sixths. 3/4 (add 1 to both) is more than 2/3." ``` Picture the bar split into 3 parts. What happens if each part is cut in half? ## Run: match the bars ```step stage: run insight: "Matching the shaded amount with 6 parts shows that splitting every part multiplies both the number of parts and the number shaded." try: { playground: board, starter: "bars.yml#run", height: 520 } check: { type: board, text: "The top bar is $\\tfrac{2}{3}$. Set the orange bar to 6 parts ($d = 6$) and shade the same amount. Was your prediction right?", when: "e = 1 and d = 6" } ``` $d$ is the number of parts in the orange bar and $c$ the number shaded. The board says when the two shade the same amount. ## Investigate: multiply or divide both ```step stage: investigate insight: "Multiplying or dividing the top and the bottom by the same number keeps the amount; dividing by the highest common factor gives lowest terms in one step. Lily's mistake adds the same number to both." tasks: - check: type: answer q: "Write $\\tfrac{12}{18}$ in its simplest form." answer: "2/3" form: simplest feedback: - ["6/9", "That is equal, but 6 and 9 still share 3. Divide again, or divide by 6 in one go."] - ["4/6", "That is equal, but 4 and 6 still share 2."] explain: "The highest common factor of 12 and 18 is 6: 12 ÷ 6 = 2 and 18 ÷ 6 = 3, so 2/3." - check: type: bug code: "working.txt#lily" text: "Lily looks for a fraction equal to $\\tfrac{2}{3}$. Click the line where her working goes wrong." answer: 3 fault: logic misconception: fraction-add-same explain: "Line 3: adding changes the amount (3/4 is more than 2/3). Doing the same to the top and the bottom means multiplying or dividing: 2/3 = 4/6." - check: type: question q: "Why is $\\tfrac{2}{3} = \\tfrac{8}{12}$?" options: ["Each third is split into 4 twelfths, so 2 thirds are 8 twelfths", "8 − 2 = 6 and 12 − 3 = 9", "8 and 12 are both even"] answer: 0 feedback: [null, "Subtracting does not tell you about the amount.", "Many fractions with even numbers are not equal to 2/3, such as 4/12."] explain: "× 4 on the top and the bottom: the same amount, cut into 4 times as many parts." ``` ### Simplest form Here is how to find equivalent fractions, and the simplest one. ```worked \tfrac{2}{3} = \tfrac{2 \times 4}{3 \times 4} = \tfrac{8}{12} :: Split each part into 4: multiply the top and the bottom by 4. \tfrac{12}{18} = \tfrac{12 \div 2}{18 \div 2} = \tfrac{6}{9} :: Join parts: divide the top and the bottom by a common factor. \tfrac{6}{9} = \tfrac{6 \div 3}{9 \div 3} = \tfrac{2}{3} :: 6 and 9 still share 3, so divide again. \tfrac{12}{18} = \tfrac{12 \div 6}{18 \div 6} = \tfrac{2}{3} :: Or in one step: divide by the highest common factor, 6. ``` A fraction is in **simplest form** (lowest terms) when the top and the bottom have no common factor but 1. Try one: simplify $\tfrac{12}{18}$. ### Find the mistake Read Lily's working. What does "the same" have to mean? ### Why they are equal ## Modify: one change at a time ```step stage: modify insight: "One change at a time: a different fraction on the board, a missing number, simplifying, simplifying on the board, then the edge case of a fraction already in lowest terms." try: { playground: board, starter: "bars.yml#twelfths", height: 520 } tasks: - starter: "bars.yml#twelfths" hint: "Each quarter split into 3 makes twelfths." check: { type: board, text: "The top bar is $\\tfrac{3}{4}$. Make the orange bar an equal fraction with 12 parts.", when: "e = 1 and d = 12", explain: "3/4 = 9/12: × 3 on the top and the bottom." } - check: type: answer q: "Fill the gap: $\\tfrac{3}{5} = \\tfrac{?}{20}$." answer: "12" feedback: - ["18", "5 → 20 is × 4, not + 15. Multiply the top by 4 too."] - ["3", "The bottom was multiplied by 4. Do the same to the top."] explain: "5 × 4 = 20, so 3 × 4 = 12." - check: type: answer q: "Write $\\tfrac{15}{25}$ in its simplest form." answer: "3/5" form: simplest feedback: - ["15/25", "15 and 25 share 5."] explain: "Divide by 5: 3/5." - starter: "bars.yml#simplify" hint: ["Make d smaller: try 6 parts, then 3.", "Keep the same amount shaded."] check: { type: board, text: "The top bar is $\\tfrac{8}{12}$. Make the orange bar the same amount with as few parts as possible.", when: "e = 1 and s = 1", explain: "8/12 = 2/3: divide by 4, the highest common factor." } - check: type: question q: "Edge case: can $\\tfrac{7}{9}$ be simplified?" options: ["No: 7 and 9 have no common factor but 1", "Yes: 7/9 = 1/2", "Yes: divide both by 7"] answer: 0 feedback: [null, "7/9 is more than a half.", "9 ÷ 7 is not a whole number."] explain: "7 and 9 share no factor but 1, so 7/9 is already in simplest form." ``` ### Twelfths Each task changes one thing. ### A missing number ### Simplify ### Fewest parts ### Already simplest ## Practise: equal fractions ```step stage: practise insight: "Simplifying, finding a missing number and comparing with a common denominator, mixed; adding to both is the planted slip; the review keeps integers fresh." tasks: - check: type: answer q: "Write $\\tfrac{18}{24}$ in its simplest form." answer: "3/4" form: simplest feedback: - ["9/12", "9 and 12 still share 3."] - ["6/8", "6 and 8 still share 2."] explain: "HCF 6: 18 ÷ 6 = 3 and 24 ÷ 6 = 4." smaller: check: { type: "number", q: "What's the biggest number that goes into both 18 and 24?", answer: 6, explain: "6. Divide the top and the bottom by 6." } - check: type: answer q: "Fill the gap: $\\tfrac{5}{8} = \\tfrac{15}{?}$." answer: "24" feedback: - ["18", "5 → 15 is × 3, not + 10."] explain: "× 3: 8 × 3 = 24." - check: type: question q: "Which is bigger, $\\tfrac{2}{3}$ or $\\tfrac{3}{5}$? Write both with 15 parts." options: ["2/3 (10/15 is more than 9/15)", "3/5 (it has bigger numbers)", "They are equal"] answer: 0 feedback: [null, "Bigger numbers do not mean a bigger amount: 3/5 = 9/15.", "2/3 = 10/15 and 3/5 = 9/15."] explain: "2/3 = 10/15 and 3/5 = 9/15, so 2/3 is bigger." - check: type: answer q: "Review: work out $-3 + 5$." answer: "2" feedback: - ["-8", "Adding 5 moves right from −3."] explain: "Start at −3 and move 5 right: 2." ``` ### Simplify ### Missing number ### Compare ### Review: integers ## Make: neither in lowest terms ```step stage: make insight: "Building two equal fractions where neither is in lowest terms shows that one amount has many names, all multiples of its simplest one." try: { playground: board, starter: "bars.yml#make", height: 560 } hint: ["Start with a simple fraction such as 1/2 and multiply its top and bottom by 2 for one bar.", "Multiply by 3 for the other bar."] check: { type: board, text: "Make the two bars equal, with neither fraction in lowest terms.", when: "e = 1 and t = 0 and s = 0", explain: "For example 2/4 and 3/6, or 4/6 and 8/12: both simplify to the same fraction." } ``` Then: what is the simplest form of both your fractions? ## Make: a pizza on paper ```step stage: make insight: "Dividing the top and the bottom by the highest common factor is the move; the paper task makes them say why that number and not just any common factor." hint: ["What is the biggest number that goes into both 8 and 12?", "Divide the top and the bottom by it."] check: type: reasoning paper: true q: "A pizza is cut into 12 equal slices and 8 slices are eaten. Write the fraction eaten in simplest form. What is its bottom number?" steps: - ["$\\tfrac{8}{12}$ of the pizza was eaten", "8 of the 12 equal slices"] - ["The highest common factor of 8 and 12 is $4$", "4 is the biggest number that divides both"] - ["$\\tfrac{8 \\div 4}{12 \\div 4} = \\tfrac{2}{3}$", "divide the top and the bottom by the same number: the amount stays the same"] - ["$\\tfrac{2}{3}$, which is 4 slices out of 6 if the same pizza is cut into sixths", "check: $\\tfrac{4}{6} = \\tfrac{2}{3}$, the same amount"] picks: - step: 2 q: "Why divide the top and the bottom by 4?" options: - "4 is the biggest number that divides both 8 and 12, so one step reaches the simplest form" - "4 is the difference between 8 and 12" - "Any number works, as long as you subtract it from the top and the bottom" answer: 0 feedback: [null, "The difference has nothing to do with it. Look for a number that divides both.", "Subtracting changes the amount: 8 − 2 = 6 over 12 − 2 = 10 is a different fraction. Divide, don't subtract."] answer: 3 feedback: - [12, "That is the bottom of 8/12, which is not in simplest form yet. Divide the top and the bottom by 4."] - [6, "That is the bottom of 4/6, which still simplifies: divide the top and the bottom by 2."] criteria: - "I wrote the fraction first, 8 out of 12." - "I divided the top and the bottom by the same number." - "My answer cannot be simplified any more." explain: "8 of 12 slices is 8/12. The highest common factor of 8 and 12 is 4, so divide both by 4: 2/3. Four of six slices is the same amount." ``` Do this one in your book, not on the screen. The pizza is made up for the task, but the question is real: the same amount can be named by many fractions, and a simplest form is the one that is easy to compare. Write the fraction, find the highest common factor, and type the simplest form. ```teacher summary: Students match shaded amounts on fraction bars to find equivalent fractions, learn that multiplying or dividing the top and the bottom by the same number keeps the amount, and simplify by the highest common factor (AC9M7N04, node 1). time: 40 timing: Predict and Run 8 min · Investigate 12 min · Modify 10 min · Practise and Make 10 min goals: - I can find equivalent fractions by multiplying or dividing the top and the bottom by the same number. - I can write a fraction in its simplest form using the highest common factor. - I can explain with a picture why two fractions are equal. struggle: Adding or subtracting the same number to the top and the bottom (2/3 becoming 3/4). Ask them to shade both bars and compare the amounts; the bars disagree. before: > Do the Run board yourself first. Students need fractions as parts of a whole (Year 6) and factors and highest common factors (Year 7 Number). The one idea: equal fractions shade the same amount; the same multiplication or division on the top and the bottom keeps the amount. The common mistake is adding the same number to both (2/3 = 3/4); it is planted in Lily's working. Simplest-form answers are marked by form: an equal fraction that can still be simplified is told so, not marked right. running: - "Predict: take a show of hands. Students who chose 3/4 added 1 to both." - "Run: ask what happened to each third when the orange bar went to 6 parts." - "Investigate: model the worked example with the bars: split each part (multiply), join parts (divide)." - "Modify: before the fewest-parts task, ask: how will you know you cannot join any more?" - "Make: collect pairs and ask for the simplest form of each." - "Paper: the pizza is worked in books; the page marks the answer (2/3) and why the top and the bottom are divided by 4. Books out, then look for the highest common factor named before any dividing." stuck: - see: A student adds the same number to the top and the bottom (Lily's mistake). ask: Set both on the bars. Is the same amount shaded? fix: "Same means the same multiplication or division: 2/3 = 4/6." - see: A student simplifies in steps and stops too early (6/9 for 12/18). ask: Do the top and the bottom still share a factor? fix: Keep dividing, or divide by the highest common factor once. - see: A student cannot find the missing number in 3/5 = ?/20. ask: What was the bottom multiplied by? fix: Do the same to the top. stretch: Find all the fractions equal to 3/4 with a bottom number less than 50. What do their bottoms have in common? support: Use the bars for every question; physical fraction walls help too. leads: > Next: Fractions, decimals and percentages (node 2), then Fractions and decimals on the line (node 3). Where it leads: adding and subtracting fractions with different denominators (common denominators), and ratio. exit: q: Write 20/32 in its simplest form, and give one other fraction equal to it. a: 5/8 (÷ 4). For example 10/16 or 15/24. explain: > Fractions are **equivalent** when they name the same amount. Multiply or divide the top and the bottom (the numerator and the denominator) by the **same** number: $\tfrac{2}{3} = \tfrac{2 \times 4}{3 \times 4} = \tfrac{8}{12}$. (Adding the same number to both changes the amount.) A fraction is in **simplest form** when the top and the bottom share no factor but 1. Divide both by their highest common factor: $\tfrac{12}{18} = \tfrac{2}{3}$ (÷ 6). ```

# region: lily
Find a fraction equal to 2/3.
Do the same to the top and the bottom.
Add 1 to the top and add 1 to the bottom.
So 2/3 = 3/4.
